title: DHCP
summary: The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) lets a client that has no address ask a local server for one, and receive an address, a subnet mask, a default gateway, name server addresses and other options for a fixed lease period. The exchange is a four step conversation, usually described as discover, offer, request and acknowledge, and it runs over the local link using broadcast before the client has any routable address at all. Because that reply arrives before any trust has been established, an unauthorised server on the same segment can hand out a gateway that redirects traffic, a false name server, or an address range that causes a denial of service. The standard defence is DHCP snooping on access switches, which permits server replies only from trusted ports and can bind a client address to a switch port. The common mistake is assuming a switched network is safe by default, when anything on the same broadcast domain can answer first.

beginner.definition: DHCP stands for Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol. It is the service that gives a device an address when it joins a network. Along with the address, it can send the gateway, the name servers and other settings. The address is lent for a set time, called a lease.
beginner.whyItMatters: Without this service, someone would set an address on every device by hand, and mistakes would be common. Two devices with the same address cannot both work properly. The service also saves time when devices move between offices. But a device trusts the first answer it receives, so a fake server on the same network can mislead it. That is why switches need protection on the ports where these replies arrive.
howItWorks: A new device joins the network and does not have an address yet.
It calls out to the local network, asking any server to help.
A server answers with an address and other settings it can lend.
The device accepts the offer and asks the server to confirm that address.
The server confirms the address, and the device starts using the settings.
The address returns to the pool when the lease ends or the device leaves.
beginner.example: Imagine a large hotel where guests arrive without a room number. At the front desk they ask for a room, and the clerk checks which rooms are free. The clerk hands over a key card and explains where the lift, the restaurant and the fire exit are. The card works for the length of the stay and then stops. If a stranger stood in the lobby and handed out keys first, guests would follow those directions. They would end up in the wrong place. A network needs the same care: only the real desk should hand out keys.
takeaways: A device trusts the first answer it gets, so guard the network edge.
Use switch features that only trust server replies from chosen ports.
Short leases help devices move, but plan the address range well.

objectives: Explain what DHCP does and which settings it supplies to a client.
Describe the four step exchange a client and server use on the local link.
Explain what a lease is and why addresses are borrowed rather than owned.
Identify how an unauthorised server on the same segment can mislead clients.
Describe the switch level controls that restrict where server replies may come from.
